jack-johnson.excerpt: The first Black heavyweight champion of the world, convicted over who he loved, and pardoned 72 years after he died.
sections: Galveston

John Arthur Johnson was born in Galveston, Texas, on 31 March 1878, the third of nine children of parents who had been enslaved. He had a few years of schooling, then worked on the Galveston boats and in kitchens. By sixteen he was on his own. His first fight, against a fellow longshoreman, paid a dollar and a half. He was six feet one, and they called him the Galveston Giant.
In February 1903, in Los Angeles, he won the title of Black heavyweight champion. The next year he challenged the world champion, Jim Jeffries, who refused to fight a Black man.
Sydney, 26 December 1908

Johnson chased the champion Tommy Burns across the world until promoters guaranteed Burns 30,000 dollars to fight him. On 26 December 1908, at Rushcutters Bay outside Sydney, about 20,000 people watched; few cheered for Johnson. He outweighed Burns by some 24 pounds and beat him so badly that police stopped the fight in the fourteenth round. Jack Johnson was the first Black heavyweight champion of the world.
Many white Americans were furious. Newspapers and fans called for a "Great White Hope" to take the title back.
Reno, 4 July 1910

Jim Jeffries came out of retirement to try. On 4 July 1910, in Reno, Nevada, more than 22,000 people watched what the promoter Tex Rickard billed as the Fight of the Century. Jeffries' corner gave up in the fifteenth round. Johnson earned 117,000 dollars, and Jeffries admitted he could never have beaten him even at his best. In the days after the fight, white mobs attacked Black Americans in cities across the country.
The Mann Act

Johnson lived as he pleased and refused to bow to anyone. In 1911 he married Etta Duryea, a white divorcee, who took her own life the next year; in December 1912 he married Lucille Cameron, who was also white. His relationships with white women enraged many Americans. In 1913 an all-white jury convicted him under the Mann Act, a law against taking women across state lines for "immoral purposes", in a case aimed squarely at those relationships. The judge was Kenesaw Mountain Landis, later baseball's first commissioner; the sentence was a year and a day in prison and a 1,000-dollar fine.

Free pending appeal, Johnson fled the country with his wife and spent seven years abroad, fighting for small purses in Paris, Buenos Aires, Spain and Mexico. On 5 April 1915, in Havana, at 37 and out of shape, he lost the title to Jess Willard in the 26th round. Rumours that he threw the fight have circulated ever since; nothing supports them in our sources.
Leavenworth, and a pardon

In 1920 Johnson surrendered to the United States and served about ten months in the federal prison at Leavenworth, where he boxed five exhibitions. He kept fighting into his fifties, his last sanctioned bouts in 1928. Jack Johnson died on 10 June 1946, at 68, in a car crash near Raleigh, North Carolina. In 1954 he became a charter member of the Boxing Hall of Fame.

On 24 May 2018, 72 years after his death, the President of the United States granted him a posthumous pardon for the 1913 conviction, after years of pressure from his great-great-niece, from Senators John McCain and Harry Reid, and from the boxing world. Prize-money figures for his fights differ between sources and are given here only where two agree.

jesse-owens.excerpt: Four Olympic gold medals in Berlin. Four months later he was racing a horse in Havana for money.
sections: J.C.

James Cleveland Owens was born on 12 September 1913 on a tenant farm in Oakville, Alabama, to Henry and Emma Owens, the son of a sharecropper and the grandson of an enslaved man. In 1922 the family moved north to Cleveland, where a teacher misheard his initials, J.C., as Jesse. The name stayed with him for life.

At Fairmount Junior High a track coach, Charles Riley, spotted him. At East Technical High School he equalled the world record for the 100-yard dash, 9.4 seconds, and was elected class president. He enrolled at Ohio State in 1933.
Forty-five minutes in Ann Arbor

On 25 May 1935, at the Big Ten championships in Ann Arbor, Michigan, Owens set three world records and tied a fourth within about 45 minutes: the 100-yard dash, the 220-yard dash, the 220-yard hurdles, and a long jump of 26 feet 8¼ inches that stood as the world record for 25 years. It is still called one of the greatest afternoons in the history of sport.
Berlin, 1936

At the Olympic Games in Berlin in the summer of 1936, Owens won four gold medals: the 100 metres in 10.3 seconds, the 200 metres in 20.7, the long jump with an Olympic record of 26 feet 5¼ inches, and the 4x100-metre relay, in which he, Ralph Metcalfe, Foy Draper and Frank Wykoff set a world record of 39.8 seconds. He was 22.

Two stories told about Berlin are left out here. The claim that President Roosevelt snubbed him on his return appears only in opinion columns. The story that his German rival Luz Long gave him advice in the long jump is disputed.
Racing a horse

Fame did not pay the bills. Owens never competed as an amateur again, and Ohio State ruled him ineligible for poor grades. On 26 December 1936, in Havana, Cuba, he raced against a horse for money, and for years afterwards he ran paid exhibitions, against horses, cars and baseball players, toured with the Harlem Globetrotters, and tap-danced on stage. How much he was paid in Havana is not verified, and a quote often attributed to him about not being able to eat gold medals could not be checked against a primary source.

A dry-cleaning business failed and he filed for bankruptcy in 1939. During the war the government made him director of a fitness programme for Black Americans, and from 1943 he ran personnel for Black workers at Ford in Detroit until the job ended with the war. In 1949 he moved his family to Chicago, where he built a career in public relations and public speaking.
Recognition

In 1950 sportswriters voted him the greatest track athlete of the half century. In 1955 President Eisenhower sent him abroad as a goodwill ambassador, to India, the Philippines and Malaya, and he kept making such tours for twenty years. In 1976, forty years after Berlin, President Gerald Ford gave him the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Owens had married Minnie Ruth Solomon in 1932; they had three daughters. A lifelong smoker, he was diagnosed with lung cancer in 1979 and died on 31 March 1980 at his home in Tucson, Arizona. The fastest man on earth, who had raced a horse to make a living.
